title: Rowlandton Mound Site (15McN3): Mississippian Town in McCracken County
summary: In McCracken County, the Rowlandton Mound Site (15MCN3) was a Mississippian town with a large platform mound, lived in from about 1100 to 1350 CE.
bodyMarkdown:
Around 1100 CE, people in McCracken County began building a town around a large earthen mound. For about 250 years, until roughly 1350, the Rowlandton Mound Site was a home and a civic center. It covered about three hectares, or seven and a half acres. That is roughly the size of [Wickliffe Mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wickliffe_Mounds), the best-known Mississippian town in far western Kentucky.

The town was part of the [Mississippian world](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mississippian_culture). Across the Southeast and the Midwest, corn-farming communities built [platform mounds](https://grokipedia.com/page/Platform_mound): flat-topped earthen mounds that raised important buildings above everyone else. Rowlandton had one large platform mound with a village beside it. Building a mound like this took organized work over many seasons.

That suggests leaders who could gather their neighbors to help, and a town that wanted to be seen.

For years, archaeologists had a ready explanation for towns like this. Western Kentucky civic centers such as Rowlandton, the Twin Mounds site and the Tolu site were thought to be thirteenth-century outposts of [Kincaid Mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kincaid_Mounds), a powerful center across the Ohio in southern Illinois. Excavations in 2006 by Kit Wesler of Murray State University showed that this was not the case. Instead, these centers were probably started by local [Late Woodland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Woodland_period) people, whose families had lived in the area for generations before Mississippian ways took hold.

That changes how we picture western Kentucky at the time. These weren't colonies set up by outsiders. Local communities adopted new ideas about farming, building and leadership, and changed their own landscape to match. Like many Mississippian towns in the region, Rowlandton was left behind by the mid-1300s. That was a time when people across the lower Ohio Valley were reorganizing and moving.

## Kentucky today

The site is protected, and its map pin is generalized to guard against looting. Rowlandton shows that McCracken County was home to a planned Mississippian town built by people with deep local roots, long before the river trade that later shaped the county. The best way to honor it is to learn about it from a distance.

David Pollack's account of the site is in The Archaeology of Kentucky: An Update, published by the Kentucky Heritage Council in 2008.
